evidence_quotes.quote: In 2018 the collapse of the wastewater infrastructure of Gauteng’s Emfuleni Local Municipality was responsible for a severe fish-kill in the Vaal River Barrage.
Emfuleni’s crisis was the result of almost two decades of delays and underinvestment in the maintenance and upgrade of a local wastewater system earmarked for regional service delivery.
There simply was no systemic regime of consistency on the maintenance and upgrade programme for the two local wastewater treatment works of Rietspruit and Sebokeng.
This article is based on two reports of which the first was a pro bono submission to the South African Human Rights Commission. The second report was funded by the European Union.
This study highlights the Integrated Vaal River system, the historical origins of today’s Emfuleni, and culminates with a discussion on the disaster of 2018 and its aftermath up until 2021.

criterion_notes.c1: Primary focus is an environmental and urban history (1891-2021) of sub-catchment surface-water pollution, fish kills, and bulk municipal wastewater treatment works (WWTW) collapse in the Vaal River Barrage rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. Township water/sanitation history, a cited mid-2010s 90.9% sanitation access estimate, localized hostel/street sewage backups, municipal pipeline leakage, and a Rand Water bulk-supply throttling episode appear only as incidental context within the river-pollution chronicle.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2, but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper discusses municipal governance collapse, provincial financial administration, intergovernmental interventions (DWS, Rand Water, ERWAT, SANDF), the SAHRC inquiry, High Court public-meeting orders, and Section 63 of the Water Services Act of 1997. Under the 2026-10-13 clarification, however, the paper does NOT examine a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household/community service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility/regulatory structure governing access); instead, it narrates generic WWTW maintenance/upgrade project delivery delays, capital funding shortfalls, contractor work stoppages, and macro-governance background. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper fails c1, c4, and c5.
criterion_notes.c3: Written as a chronological environmental-history narrative with no methods section, research design, or systematic data-analysis procedure reported; relies predominantly on secondary histories, government/NGO documents, and newspaper reports, though footnotes record university ethics clearance (NWU-00618-18-A7) and occasional primary audio notes from SAHRC/public meetings and key-informant phone interviews.
criterion_notes.c4: Main outcomes examined are raw sewage discharges into the Vaal River Barrage, fish kills, downstream river contamination at Parys/Vredefort Dome, and operational breakdown of WWTWs and pump stations, rather than systematically measured household or community service-access outcomes (incidental press/secondary mentions of sewage flooding in Sebokeng hostels and Rand Water's 60% bulk supply reduction are purely descriptive context).
criterion_notes.c5: No identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, or structured population-exposure-outcome framework linking a defined governance exposure to household or community water/sanitation service access across the 1891-2021 catchment narrative.

study_design: Historical narrative / environmental history case chronicle (no empirical methods section reported)
population_and_sample: Vaal River Barrage sub-catchment and Emfuleni Local Municipality in Gauteng, South Africa (no analytical sample reported)
exposure: Historical urbanisation, industrial transition, municipal maladministration, contractor work stoppages, and two decades of delays and underinvestment in maintaining and upgrading municipal wastewater treatment works
outcome: Collapse of Emfuleni wastewater treatment works (Rietspruit, Sebokeng, Leeuwkuil) and pump stations, raw sewage spills, and severe fish kills and river contamination in the Vaal River Barrage and downstream
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic): Tempelhoff (2021) is an environmental and urban history of the Vaal River Barrage sub-catchment (1891-2021) examining raw sewage pollution, fish kills, and the operational collapse of Emfuleni Local Municipality's bulk wastewater treatment works rather than household or community water/sanitation service access (which appears only tangentially in historical/descriptive passages). It also fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading because it chronicles generic WWTW maintenance/upgrade delays, capital funding shortfalls, contractor protests, and macro-governance decay rather than a rule-type mechanism governing service access, and fails Criterion 5 because it is an unstructured historical narrative without a reported empirical study design or identifiable service-access population-exposure-outcome framework (so plain_criterion2_decision is also 'exclude').
